M0B-01-IF.5:
## If it happens, then

So far every formula has always calculated the same way, whatever the numbers.
`IF` is different: it looks at a condition and **chooses** between two answers depending on whether it is
true or false. It's the first formula on the sheet that decides, not just adds.

The form is always the same, in three pieces separated by commas:

`=IF(condition, value if true, value if false)`

The condition compares two cells with an operator: `>` greater than, `<` less than, `>=`
greater than or equal, `<=` less than or equal. The difference between `>` and `>=` looks like a detail,
but it decides whether the edge case — the exact tie — passes the condition or not.

This month the team sold {p0}. The target that triggers the bonus is
{p1}: above it, the team earns {p2}; otherwise nothing.
There is also a minimum warning threshold, {p3}: falling below it (or
hitting it exactly) triggers a penalty of {p4}.

M0B-02-IFANNIDATO.5:
## When two answers aren't enough

`IF` chooses between two values. But an advisory fee scale doesn't have two bands,
it has four — and each one needs a different rate. The solution is nesting: the
"value if false" of the first IF is not a number, it's another IF, which in turn can
contain a third. You write it like this:

`=IF(condition1, value1, IF(condition2, value2, IF(condition3, value3, value4)))`

Every extra IF adds a parenthesis to close at the end: with three nested IFs you
close three together, all at the end of the formula. That's where most
errors are born — not in the logic, in counting the parentheses.

Here is the scale: below {p0} of Enterprise Value the fee is
{p1}; from there up to {p2} (excluded) it drops to {p3}; from
{p4} up to {p5} (excluded) to {p6}; from {p7}
upwards to {p8}. It's the classic pattern: the bigger the deal, the lower
the percentage — the fee in euros still grows, just more slowly.

The thresholds and rates are already written on the sheet: the formula must **reference** them,
never retype them as numbers inside the formula. If the scale changes tomorrow, you update one
cell and every fee recalculates by itself.

A warning for when there are ten bands instead of four: nesting IF ten times
is hard to read, and misplacing a parenthesis in the middle becomes almost automatic. In that
case the right function is **IFS**: `IFS(condition1, value1, condition2, value2, ...)`
lists the condition-value pairs one after the other, without nesting them — same logic
as the nested IF, but without the wall of closing parentheses. With four bands the nested IF
is perfectly readable: it's a tool worth knowing anyway, because
in a real model the bands are sometimes really ten.

M0B-03-LOGICI.5:
## When one comparison isn't enough

An investment committee never decides on a single number. Criteria combine:
"eligible if the score holds **and** revenue holds", "on alert if the margin weakens
**or** leverage breaks through". `AND`, `OR` and `NOT` live inside the condition, exactly
like a single comparison: they return TRUE or FALSE, they change nothing else.

- `AND(criterion1,criterion2,...)` is TRUE only if **every** criterion is true.
- `OR(criterion1,criterion2,...)` is TRUE if **at least one** criterion is true.
- `NOT(condition)` flips what it finds: TRUE becomes FALSE, and vice versa.

Today's target operates in the {settore} sector. The committee gave it a qualitative score
of **{p1}/100** (minimum threshold: {p2}/100) and
verified revenue of **{p3}** (minimum threshold: {p4}).
The EBITDA margin is **{p5}** (minimum threshold: {p6}), leverage
Debt/EBITDA is **{p7}** (maximum threshold: {p8}).

From these eight numbers build three verdicts: eligibility (needs everything), alert (needs
little) and exclusion (the opposite of eligibility, without redoing the maths).

Here, though, the denominator is never zero: look at it before writing the formula. Wrapping the division in IFERROR anyway isn't prudence, it's a way of not noticing the day that cell really breaks.
M0B-04-IFERROR.17:
## Don't sweep the error under the rug

Two production lines in the same plant. For each one you want the **unit cost**:
production cost divided by units produced. It's the number that tells you whether the selling price
really covers costs.

On the **{linea1}** line no unit came out this month ({motivo}), but the production
cost — {p2}, staff and depreciation already incurred — is there anyway.
Dividing it by zero units produces `#DIV/0!`. Typing a zero over it by hand would make it
vanish from view, but a model that hides its errors is worse than one that shows them:
that fake number would end up in a total, and nobody would know where it came from any more.

**`IFERROR(formula, value_if_error)`** catches the error and replaces it with something
you chose — not with something hidden by Excel. Here the list price, already
in the table, is the only defensible cost estimate when you have no production to divide by.

On the **{linea2}** line, instead, the month was normal: units produced are never
zero. IFERROR protects against nothing there, it only adds a fallback value that will never
kick in — until one day, for a reason you didn't foresee, it kicks in without
you noticing. Use IFERROR where an error is a real possibility, not everywhere out of habit.
M0B-04-IFERROR.24: IFERROR(B4/C4, D4): the first argument is the formula that can fail, the second is what to return when it really fails.
M0B-04-IFERROR.25: The fallback must come from D4, not from a number typed by hand: that's the price you defend in the meeting.
M0B-04-IFERROR.26: B5/C5, without IFERROR: here the denominator is never zero, there's no error to catch.
M0B-04-IFERROR.title: The error that doesn't hide

M0B-05-CROSSSHEET.6:
## A model lives on several sheets

Here the income statement is split across two sheets: **Model**, where you work, and **"{FOGLIO_DATI}"**,
which holds another line item. It's not an odd case: that's how almost every
real model is built, with line items spread across sheets that talk to each other.

So far a cell was just called `B2`, because the sheet you were writing in was obvious.
When the cell you need is on **another sheet**, that obviousness disappears: you have to say it,
with the `Sheet!Cell` syntax — for example `Model!B2`.

The "{FOGLIO_DATI}" sheet, though, has a space in its name. If you write `Income Statement!B2` without
quotes, Excel reads two separate words and gets lost. The rule: **if the sheet name
contains a space (or almost anything that isn't a letter, digit or underscore),
it must be wrapped in single quotes**: `'Income Statement'!B2`. On the sheet you're already in,
though, you never need any of that: `B2` is enough, exactly as before.

Starting numbers: revenue {p1}, operating costs {p2} — both in Model.
Interest expense is in the other sheet and you'll only see it by opening it.

M0B-06-NAMEDRANGES.12:
## A name instead of an address

When you write `$C$2` inside a formula you're saying "this cell, always this one, never
move". It works — you've already practised it. But whoever rereads the formula six months from now has to go
to C2 to find out what it holds.

In real Excel there's a more readable way: give that cell **a name**, with **Formulas >
Define Name**, or by typing the name straight into the **Name box** — the field to the left
of the formula bar where you usually read an address like "C2" — and pressing Enter. From then on
`=B6*$C$2` is written `=B6*SharePrice`: the formula reads by itself without having to go
and check what's inside, and if you ever move the cell the name follows it.

*(This trainer doesn't create real named ranges in the sheet yet — that's future work on the
game engine. The exercise still trains exactly the discipline that makes them useful:
spotting the single cell that every formula must share, and locking it with `$` so
it doesn't slide when you copy it.)*

## The case

handling the closing keeps a fee of **{p1}** on each shareholder's gross
before passing on the net.

Price and fee sit in **just two cells**, boxed at the top: they're the two numbers that
every row of the {p2}-shareholder table must look at — never anywhere else on the sheet,
never a value retyped by hand row by row.

M0B-07-CONSISTENZARIGA.10:
## One row, one formula, no exceptions

A revenue projection isn't five independent numbers: it's **one formula**, written
once and dragged across the whole horizon. If you wrote it well, every cell in the row
tells the same story — "the year before, grown by the rate" — just shifted by one column.

Here Year 0 revenue is **{p0}** and grows at a fixed rate of
**{p1}** a year, for {ANNI_PROIEZIONE} years. The rate is in **a single cell**,
boxed in C3: it's that one, and no other, that every column of the row must reference
with the same absolute anchor.

**Fill down** (Ctrl+D) copies downwards, **fill right** (Ctrl+R) copies to the right, and if
you first select the whole area and then type the formula in the first cell, **Ctrl+Enter**
pastes it into the whole selection in one go. Three shortcuts for the same gesture: take a
correct formula and make it flow.

Why it matters so much that it stays IDENTICAL: nobody plants an error in a model by writing
a wrong formula across the whole row — it would show at a glance. They plant it by **touching up
a single cell in the middle**, maybe to fix a number that looked odd, maybe
pasting a value over the formula during a last-minute change. The total
keeps calculating, no red hash appears, and the number looks plausible: it's
the most common silent error in real models, because you only see it by comparing the FORMULAS
cell by cell — never by looking only at the numbers they return.
